mcq.q: In Zimmerman (2002), how is self-regulation described most accurately?
o: A fixed learning style that a learner either has or does not have
A separate academic skill taught as an independent subject
An innate intellectual ability that determines a learner's grades
A self-directive process by which learners turn mental abilities into learning skills
mcq.e: The paper: "Self-regulation refers to self-generated thoughts, feelings, and behaviors that are oriented to attaining goals", and it is "a self-directive process by which learners transform their mental abilities into task-related skills". It is not a mental ability or an academic skill.

mcq.q: What is the character Tracy in the paper's opening used to illustrate?
o: A student with a learning disorder needing medical diagnosis
A lazy student who lacks innate mathematical ability
A student lacking self-regulation: no specific goals
A gifted student who uses every learning strategy skillfully
mcq.e: Tracy studies inefficiently: no specific goals, no plan, last-minute cramming, vague self-evaluation, and she blames failure on "lack of ability". She is the mirror image of a self-regulated learner.

mcq.q: According to Zimmerman (2002), how is learning viewed in the SRL perspective?
o: As a passive process that occurs whenever the teacher lectures well enough
As an outcome that depends only on the intellectual ability already present
As something students do for themselves, not something that happens to them
As an automatic response to stimuli in the classroom environment
mcq.e: The paper stresses that learning is "something students do for themselves in a proactive way", not "something that happens to them in reaction to teaching".

mcq.q: Which benefit of SRL does Zimmerman (2002) mention for the workplace and life beyond school?
o: Learners score higher on every standardized exam
Learners need not set goals because work already comes with goals
Learners no longer need to seek help from colleagues
Learners can teach themselves new positions
mcq.e: The paper points to the need for continuous self-directed learning at work and in self-employment; SRL is central to lifelong learning.

mcq.q: What did research on experts (Ericsson and Charness 1994), cited by Zimmerman (2002), show?
o: Experts learn and practice about four hours a day
Experts practice a lot but need no special motivation
Experts practice only about one hour a day thanks to talent
Experts rely on innate gifts so hours of practice do not matter
mcq.e: The paper: experts practice about four hours a day, and the amount and quality of practice strongly predict the level of expertise reached.

mcq.q: Which view does Zimmerman (2002) reject when discussing SRL?
o: That SRL is the selective use of processes rather than a fixed trait
That SRL is asocial and self-regulated students never turn to others
That SRL includes both motivational and cognitive aspects
That SRL can be taught and varies across tasks
mcq.e: The paper says self-regulated students often actively seek help from others; the "self" is in initiative, persistence and adaptive skill, not social isolation.

mcq.q: According to Zimmerman, Bonner and Kovach (1996), cited in the paper, what is the state of classroom practice?
o: Teachers regularly teach self-regulation strategies in every subject
Teachers rarely prepare students to learn on their own: they seldom allow choices of task or method or encourage goal setting
Teachers teach all three phases but students refuse to apply them
Teachers teach SRL only to high-achieving students in the final grades
mcq.e: Zimmerman (2002) points out that few teachers prepare students for self-directed learning; they seldom let students choose tasks, methods or partners, or encourage goals and strategy instruction.

mcq.q: Which feature shows SRL is a process rather than a fixed trait?
o: Learners have the same high SRL in every subject and situation
SRL appears only after a learner has scored high on a previous exam
SRL changes only when the learner changes school or teacher
Learners use processes selectively, adapt them to each task
mcq.e: Zimmerman (2002) says SRL is not a trait that people have or lack; it is the selective use of processes and it can be taught.

mcq.q: Zimmerman (1990) found three features common to SRL definitions. Which set is right?
o: Use of SRL strategies, a self-oriented feedback loop about effectiveness, and motivation tied to learning
Goal setting, frequent exams and external rewards
Long-term memory, processing speed and emotion control
Good teachers, good textbooks and small classes
mcq.e: The three features: (1) use of SRL strategies, (2) a self-oriented feedback loop about learning effectiveness, (3) motivation related to learning, interdependent with the other two.

mcq.q: What is an "SRL strategy" in Zimmerman (1990)?
o: Study habits formed by copying classmates
Actions and processes directed at acquiring information or skill, with awareness of the link between strategy and outcome
School rules about how students must study at home
Tricks for guessing answers on multiple-choice tests
mcq.e: SRL strategies are actions and processes directed at acquiring information or skill, involving purpose and instrumentality perceived by the learner.

mcq.q: What does the "self-oriented feedback loop" mean?
o: The teacher grades work and returns the score so students know where they stand
Learners monitor how effective their learning is
Students compare their scores with classmates to find their rank
Students receive external rewards after each task
mcq.e: In Zimmerman (1990), it is a loop in which learners monitor the effectiveness of their methods and react, from changing self-perceptions to changing behavior or strategy.

mcq.q: Why is motivation counted as the third feature of SRL?
o: Because motivation determines innate intellectual ability
Because motivation appears only after a learner has scored high
Self-regulation takes time, vigilance and effort
Because motivation is an external reward given by the teacher
mcq.e: The paper says self-regulation requires preparation time and effort; skill and will are integrated parts, and learning and motivation are interdependent.

mcq.q: What does Bandura add about feedback in SRL (cited by Zimmerman 1990)?
o: Feedback can also be positive: learners raise the goal after reaching it
Feedback should occur only after the whole lesson has ended
Feedback works only when it comes from a teacher or adult
Feedback must always be corrective, never praise
mcq.e: The feedback loop is not only error correction; Bandura stresses positive feedback, where after reaching a goal learners raise their own standard.

mcq.q: According to Zimmerman (1990), in which three dimensions does a self-regulated learner participate actively?
o: Emotion, physical ability and social skills
Memory, attention and perception
Metacognition, motivation and behavior
Theory, practice and exams
mcq.e: Self-regulated learners are active in metacognition (planning, goal setting, self-monitoring, self-evaluation), motivation (confidence, attribution, interest) and behavior (selecting, structuring and creating learning environments).

mcq.q: Which of these belongs to the "behavior" dimension of a self-regulated learner?
o: Making a weekly study plan and setting long-term goals
Believing in one's own ability and seeing learning as valuable
Evaluating results against the original goal
Selecting, structuring and creating a learning environment
mcq.e: In Zimmerman (1990), the behavioral dimension covers choosing, structuring and creating learning environments, seeking advice, self-instruction and self-reward.

mcq.q: What are the three phases of Zimmerman's (2002) cyclical self-regulation model?
o: Encoding, storage and retrieval
Forethought, performance
Observation, imitation and self-control
Planning, testing and grading
mcq.e: Zimmerman (2002) describes three cyclical phases: forethought (preparation), performance, and self-reflection.

mcq.q: What are the two main process groups of the forethought phase?
o: Modeling and coaching
Self-judgment and self-reaction
Self-control and self-observation
Task analysis and self-motivation beliefs
mcq.e: Forethought has task analysis (goal setting, strategic planning) and self-motivation beliefs (self-efficacy, outcome expectations, intrinsic interest, learning-goal orientation).

mcq.q: To which group do goal setting and strategic planning belong?
o: Self-judgment in the self-reflection phase
Self-reaction in the self-reflection phase
Task analysis in the forethought phase
Self-observation in the performance phase
mcq.e: Task analysis belongs to forethought and contains two main processes: goal setting and strategic planning.

mcq.q: In the paper's spelling example, which planning strategy is named?
o: Asking the teacher to repeat the dictation many times
Reading the word list aloud to a classmate
Splitting words into syllables to learn them part by part
Copying each word a hundred times in a notebook
mcq.e: The example names planning the use of a strategy, splitting words into syllables, for a spelling word list.

mcq.q: Which four factors are self-motivation beliefs in the forethought phase?
o: Grades, rankings, rewards and teacher praise
Self-efficacy, outcome expectations, intrinsic interest
Memory, attention, processing speed and reasoning ability
Free time, books, equipment and a quiet room
mcq.e: The paper lists self-efficacy, outcome expectations, intrinsic interest or valuing, and learning-goal orientation as self-motivation beliefs.

mcq.q: What are the two main process groups of the performance phase?
o: Self-judgment and self-reaction
Modeling and coaching
Self-control and self-observation
Task analysis and self-motivation beliefs
mcq.e: Performance has self-control (imagery, self-instruction, attention focusing, task strategies) and self-observation (self-recording, self-experimentation).

mcq.q: Remembering "pan" through the image of a bread pan is an example of which process?
o: Imagery within self-control
Goal setting within task analysis
Causal attribution within self-judgment
Self-evaluation within self-judgment
mcq.e: The paper uses imagery, a self-control process, as the example of picturing "pan" as a bread pan to remember the word.

mcq.q: Choosing a study spot away from noise is an example of which process?
o: A defensive reaction, part of self-reaction
Self-experimentation, part of self-observation
Attention focusing, part of self-control
Outcome expectation, part of motivation beliefs
mcq.e: Attention focusing, such as removing distractions and choosing a place to study, belongs to self-control in the performance phase.

mcq.q: Recording study time and experimenting (studying alone versus with a friend) belong to which group?
o: Self-judgment in the self-reflection phase
Self-control in the performance phase
Task analysis in the forethought phase
Self-observation in the performance phase
mcq.e: Self-observation has self-recording and self-experimentation, such as studying alone and with a friend to see which helps.

mcq.q: What are the two main process groups of the self-reflection phase?
o: Self-control and self-observation
Self-judgment and self-reaction
Task analysis and self-motivation beliefs
Self-evaluation and material self-reward
mcq.e: Self-reflection has self-judgment (self-evaluation, attribution) and self-reaction (satisfaction, affect, adaptive or defensive reactions).

mcq.q: How many kinds of self-evaluation standards are named, and what are they?
o: Only against the teacher and against the class average
Only against the school's long-term goals
Against the textbook and against the answer key
Against one's earlier level, against others
mcq.e: Zimmerman (2002) names the standards: one's own previous level, the performance of others, and an absolute (mastery) standard.

mcq.q: How does an "adaptive" reaction differ from a "defensive" one?
o: Adaptive occurs only after success; defensive only after failure
Adaptive means reusing the same old strategy; defensive means changing strategy entirely
Adaptive means fixing or dropping a poor strategy; defensive means avoiding learning
Adaptive means trying harder; defensive means seeking help from friends
mcq.e: The paper: adaptive reactions aim to improve the method, while defensive ones aim to avoid embarrassment, such as dropping out or skipping the test.

mcq.q: Why does attributing failure to "lack of ability" reduce motivation?
o: It implies that further effort would be futile
It makes the student set goals that are too hard next time
It makes the student forget what was learned
It makes teachers reduce the support given to the student
mcq.e: Zimmerman (2002): attributing to fixed ability lowers motivation; attributing to a strategy (controllable) preserves motivation because changing strategy might succeed.

mcq.q: Which attribution helps learners keep their motivation better?
o: To innate ability that cannot be changed
To the use of a strategy or method that can be changed
To luck or random difficulty of the exam
To unfairness on the part of the marker
mcq.e: Attributing to strategy means attributing to a controllable process, implying a change of strategy could succeed next time.

mcq.q: What does the "cyclical" nature of Zimmerman's model mean?
o: Learners must repeat the same task until they reach full marks
Teachers must repeat a lesson three times so that students remember
The results of the self-reflection phase influence preparation for the next learning attempt
The three phases must always take place within a single hour
mcq.e: The paper: self-reactions from a previous attempt affect the next preparation; for example dissatisfaction leads to low self-efficacy and less effort.

mcq.q: What does Zimmerman and Kitsantas (1999) show, as cited?
o: High correlations between the use of processes across all three phases
Only the forethought phase affects learning outcomes
The three phases are empirically independent
The self-reflection phase is unrelated to self-efficacy
mcq.e: The paper reports that processes in the three phases correlate highly, supporting the cyclical nature of the model.

mcq.q: What does Bandura and Schunk (1981) support?
o: Goals imposed by the teacher are always better than self-set goals
Self-efficacy is unaffected by how goals are set
Setting specific, near goals goes with more self-observation
The vaguer and more distant the goal, the more effort learners make
mcq.e: Zimmerman (2002) cites Bandura and Schunk: specific, proximal goals go with self-observation, achievement and self-efficacy.

mcq.q: What is typical of a novice regarding goals and plans?
o: Goals set by others that are always reached
Hierarchical goals from process to outcome and careful preparation
Clear goals but no plan for carrying them out
Vague goals, poor-quality preparation
mcq.e: Novices set few specific goals, prepare poorly and regulate in a reactive way.

mcq.q: How do experts typically set goals?
o: Only outcome goals such as a score
Vaguely, such as "do my best"
They set no goals because the task is familiar
Hierarchically from process to outcome
mcq.e: Zimmerman (2002): experts set hierarchical goals from process to outcome (for example splitting an essay into introduction, body and conclusion).

mcq.q: How do novices typically judge their own results?
o: By comparison with others, so standards rise whenever someone does better
They do not judge, because they believe every result is worthwhile
By comparison with their own goals and previous progress
By an absolute standard of the subject
mcq.e: The paper: novices usually judge themselves against others, which is hard to satisfy because someone is always better; experts use their own goals.

mcq.q: What do experts mainly attribute failure to?
o: An exam too hard for the curriculum
A strategy or method that did not fit
Unfair marking by the teacher
A lack of innate ability in the subject
mcq.e: Novices attribute to lack of ability (normative), while experts attribute to strategy, which helps them keep improving.

mcq.q: What are the emotional and motivational consequences for experts compared with novices?
o: More satisfaction and continued improvement
Less satisfaction because their standards are too high
No consequences, since emotion does not affect learning
The same satisfaction, since both reach the same score
mcq.e: Novices are less satisfied and react defensively; experts are more satisfied and their self-efficacy, outcome expectations and intrinsic interest grow.

mcq.q: A graphic organizer filled with key information is an example of what for experts?
o: Evaluating oneself against others
A defensive reaction to failure
Attributing success to luck
Planning with a powerful strategy
mcq.e: The paper uses a graphic organizer filled with key information as an expert's strong strategy whose effect is tracked.

mcq.q: Why do novices often fail to monitor their learning systematically?
o: Because they are so good they do not need to monitor
With no specific goals there is no standard to monitor against
Because monitoring is forbidden in ordinary classrooms
Because they believe scores depend entirely on luck
mcq.e: Without a specific goal there is nothing to compare against, so novices track little in a systematic way (Zimmerman 2002).

mcq.q: What instrument did Zimmerman and Martinez-Pons use to collect data on SRL strategies?
mcq.sec: Zimmerman and Martinez-Pons: 14 strategies and the evidence
o: A structured interview with learning scenarios
Direct observation of students in a laboratory
A questionnaire with four choices per item
A standardized end-of-year achievement test
mcq.e: They used structured interviews with learning scenarios and let students state their own strategies; self-generated answers were preferred over multiple choice as closer to natural conditions.

mcq.q: Why did they choose open interviews over multiple choice?
mcq.sec: Zimmerman and Martinez-Pons: 14 strategies and the evidence
o: Self-generated answers simulate more closely the conditions in
Because multiple choice always gives wrong results and cannot be used
Because students cannot read multiple-choice questions
Because open interviews take less time than questionnaires
mcq.e: The paper explains that free responses better reflect how students really cope with a situation.

mcq.q: Which of these is a scenario in the interview?
mcq.sec: Zimmerman and Martinez-Pons: 14 strategies and the evidence
o: "Solve the following quadratic equation and explain your method."
"Tell us your math score from last term."
"Do you like the teacher of this subject?"
"It is hard to finish homework because something more interesting is on: how do you motivate yourself?"
mcq.e: One scenario asks how students motivate themselves when homework competes with a more attractive activity.

mcq.q: Which of these is NOT among the SRL strategy categories that were coded?
mcq.sec: Zimmerman and Martinez-Pons: 14 strategies and the evidence
o: Asking parents to do all the homework
Environmental structuring
Goal setting and planning
Self-evaluating
mcq.e: The 14 strategies include self-evaluating, organizing and transforming, goal setting and planning, seeking information, keeping records, self-monitoring, environmental structuring, self-consequences, rehearsing and memorizing, seeking social assistance and reviewing. Having someone else do the work is not an SRL strategy.

mcq.q: Who is included in "seeking social assistance"?
mcq.sec: Zimmerman and Martinez-Pons: 14 strategies and the evidence
o: Only the desk partner
Only a paid tutor
Only the homeroom teacher
Peers, teachers
mcq.e: The category "seeking social assistance" is split into asking peers, teachers and adults.

mcq.q: What does "reviewing" cover in the strategy list?
mcq.sec: Zimmerman and Martinez-Pons: 14 strategies and the evidence
o: Looking again at one's own school application
Looking at related scientific articles
Looking at the whole class's grade sheet
Looking back at notes, textbooks
mcq.e: Reviewing covers reviewing notes, textbooks and old tests.

mcq.q: How many students were in the 1986 study and how were they divided?
mcq.sec: Zimmerman and Martinez-Pons: 14 strategies and the evidence
o: 80 students: 40 in an advanced track
40 students: 20 boys and 20 girls
100 students: 50 in grade 5 and 50 in grade 8
93 students, all in the advanced track
mcq.e: Zimmerman and Martinez-Pons (1986) used 80 high-school students, 40 in the advanced track and 40 in the lower track.

mcq.q: What percentage of students did discriminant analysis classify correctly into their track in the 1986 study?
mcq.sec: Zimmerman and Martinez-Pons: 14 strategies and the evidence
mcq.e: Weighted strategy scores predicted the track of 93% of the students.

mcq.q: What does the 93% mean when the sample is split 40/40?
mcq.sec: Zimmerman and Martinez-Pons: 14 strategies and the evidence
o: It is below chance so strategies are useless
It is far above the roughly 50% chance level
It holds only for male students in the sample
It equals the chance level so it has no meaning
mcq.e: With equal groups, random guessing gives about 50%; 93% shows strategy scores separate the two groups well.

mcq.q: Of the 14 strategies, which one did NOT differ significantly between tracks?
mcq.sec: Zimmerman and Martinez-Pons: 14 strategies and the evidence
o: Self-evaluating
Environmental structuring
Keeping records
Goal setting and planning
mcq.e: The paper: advanced-track students reported significantly more use of every strategy except self-evaluating.

mcq.q: What form did the lower track's "reactive" answers take in the interview?
mcq.sec: Zimmerman and Martinez-Pons: 14 strategies and the evidence
o: "I set my own deadlines"
"I do what the teacher says"
"I make my own weekly review plan"
"I ask a friend to explain it again"
mcq.e: "Reactive" answers show students passively waiting for direction, unlike proactive strategies.

mcq.q: What do the lower track's "will" answers ("I try harder") show?
mcq.sec: Zimmerman and Martinez-Pons: 14 strategies and the evidence
o: They use strategies better than the advanced track
They lack the verbal skill to express themselves
They have many strategies but do not dare to say them
They say "try harder" without naming a method
mcq.e: The paper explains that such non-SRL answers reflect lack of initiative, not poor ability to express.

mcq.q: In the 1988 study, teacher ratings and standardized scores were factor analyzed. What resulted?
mcq.sec: Zimmerman and Martinez-Pons: 14 strategies and the evidence
o: No significant factor
Three independent factors, each explaining about 30%
One general-ability factor explaining 93% of the variance
One SRL factor explaining nearly 80% of the variance
mcq.e: Factor analysis showed a single SRL factor accounting for nearly 80% of the variance of the rated scores.

mcq.q: What was the correlation between self-reported strategy use and the teacher-rated SRL factor?
mcq.sec: Zimmerman and Martinez-Pons: 14 strategies and the evidence
mcq.e: Zimmerman (1990): self-reported strategy use correlated .70 with the SRL factor, separate from a general-ability factor.

mcq.q: If r = .70, what is the shared variance (r squared)?
mcq.sec: Zimmerman and Martinez-Pons: 14 strategies and the evidence
mcq.e: 0.70 times 0.70 is 0.49, i.e. about 49% shared variance.

mcq.q: What trend across grades 5, 8 and 11 was found for SRL strategies?
mcq.sec: Zimmerman and Martinez-Pons: 14 strategies and the evidence
o: The number of strategies rose from grade 5 to 8 and from grade 8 to 11
The number did not change between grades
The number of strategies declined with grade
Only grade 8 used more strategies than grade 5
mcq.e: Zimmerman (1990) reports strategy use increasing with grade, and gifted students had higher self-efficacy.

mcq.q: What do the "general-ability factor" and the "SRL factor" in the 1988 study tell us?
mcq.sec: Zimmerman and Martinez-Pons: 14 strategies and the evidence
o: SRL and general ability are one and inseparable
SRL strategy use is a separate dimension
SRL appears only in students with high general ability
SRL has nothing to do with learning outcomes
mcq.e: The paper stresses that self-reported strategy use correlates with the SRL factor, separate from a general-ability factor.

mcq.q: What did the Pressley and Ghatala research show about adults learning two strategies of different effectiveness?
o: They discover the difference only when working in a group
They do not track the difference while doing the task
They always choose the worse strategy even when prompted
They always discover the better strategy without any prompt
mcq.e: The paper: outcome monitoring does not happen spontaneously even in adults; only when prompted to track recall outcomes do they draw and use the information.

mcq.q: What did Ghatala and colleagues (1986) show children need to be taught?
o: To memorize more strategies
To monitor outcomes
To work alone without feedback
To learn faster to finish in less time
mcq.e: Teaching outcome monitoring, attribution to strategy and deciding on that basis are skills that must be taught.

mcq.q: What did Elliott-Faust and Pressley (1986) find with third graders?
o: There was no difference among the training conditions
Teaching the strategy alone was enough; adding self-monitoring did not help
Teaching self-instruction reduced comprehension because students were distracted
Teaching verbal self-instruction and self-monitoring improved comprehension
mcq.e: The paper cites research showing that adding self-instruction and self-monitoring to strategy training improves comprehension and keeps strategy use going.

mcq.q: According to Paris and Newman (cited in Zimmerman 1990), what is typical of children under 7?
o: Always underestimating their own ability
Frequent use of many sophisticated strategies
Naive and overly optimistic about their ability to learn, reflecting little
Very accurate about their own ability
mcq.e: Young children are often overly optimistic and assume effort is enough (Dweck and Elliott 1983); nearer adolescence self-perception is more accurate.

mcq.q: What did Sawyer, Graham and Harris (1989) find about strategy training packages?
o: Multi-component packages did better
The added self-regulation part gave the best and a significant effect
No package did better than strategy instruction alone
Only the self-regulation part worked, the other parts were useless
mcq.e: Zimmerman (1990) uses this example to show it is unclear which component is most essential in training studies.

mcq.q: What is the conclusion of Zimmerman (1990) about SRL training?
o: Training only one or two processes rarely has lasting effects
Only motivation needs raising, no strategy instruction is needed
Only metacognition needs teaching, motivation will follow
Teaching a single strong strategy is enough for every subject
mcq.e: The paper concludes that training should cover all three dimensions: metacognitive, motivational and behavioral.

mcq.q: What does Schunk stress about goal setting and self-efficacy (cited by Zimmerman 1990)?
o: They influence each other: goals nourish self-efficacy
The two have no relationship
Self-efficacy fully determines goals in one direction
Goals reduce self-efficacy because they create pressure
mcq.e: Zimmerman (1990) cites Schunk on the reciprocal relation: proximal, specific goals nourish self-efficacy and vice versa.

mcq.q: How many models does the Puustinen and Pulkkinen (2001) review compare, and on which criteria?
o: Five models, on theoretical background
Two models, on gender and culture
Three models, on cost, time and number of participants
Ten models, on learner age and school subject
mcq.e: The review compares the models of Boekaerts, Borkowski, Pintrich, Winne and Zimmerman on four criteria: theoretical background, definition, components, empirical research.

mcq.q: Who are the authors of the five models compared?
o: Boekaerts, Borkowski, Pintrich, Winne
Schraw, Flavell, Brown, Kluwe and Nelson
Kapur, Sweller, Collins, Brown and Paas
Bandura, Vygotsky, Piaget, Bruner and Dewey
mcq.e: The paper selects five models with plenty of empirical support from the preceding decade.

mcq.q: What is central to Boekaerts' adaptable-learning model?
o: Appraisal and several control systems: metacognitive, motivational
Four development levels: observation, emulation, self-control, self-regulation
A table of four phases times four areas
Four stages with a COPES structure in each
mcq.e: Boekaerts places appraisal at the center: positive appraisal widens resources, negative appraisal leads to ego protection.

mcq.q: Which instrument does Boekaerts use to measure motivation online before and after a task?
o: The On-line Motivation Questionnaire (OMQ)
The MSLQ questionnaire
The SRLIS interview
Trace methodology
mcq.e: Boekaerts uses the On-line Motivation Questionnaire (OMQ) before and after a learning task.

mcq.q: What are the two action modes in Boekaerts' model?
o: Individual and collective
Internal and external
Short-term and long-term
Fast, automatic (familiar situations) and conscious (new or difficult situations)
mcq.e: Boekaerts distinguishes a fast/automatic action mode for familiar situations from a conscious mode for situations needing control.

mcq.q: What is the focus of Borkowski's model?
o: Groups of four phases times four areas
Process-oriented metacognition: strategy selection and use, executive functions, the self-system
Triadic reciprocal determinism
Emotional appraisal before the task
mcq.e: Borkowski stresses process-oriented metacognition and strategy training and transfer.

mcq.q: What did Reid and Borkowski (1987) show to be the most effective training?
o: No training gave a lasting effect
Attribution training only, with no need to teach strategies
Self-control training plus attribution
Strategy training only, with the effect gone after one week
mcq.e: The study showed strategy training plus self-control and attribution gave the best effect, lasting up to 10 months.

mcq.q: How is Pintrich's framework described?
o: Four stages with a COPES structure
Three cyclical phases and four development levels
Two control systems and two action modes
Four phases (forethought, monitoring, control
mcq.e: Pintrich presents a table of four phases by four areas as a heuristic framework.

mcq.q: What are the four areas of Pintrich's framework?
o: Goals, plans, execution, evaluation
Person, behavior, environment, society
Memory, attention, language, movement
Cognition, motivation and affect
mcq.e: The four areas: cognition, motivation/affect, behavior and context.

mcq.q: Which instrument is associated with Pintrich?
o: The OMQ (On-line Motivation Questionnaire)
The MSLQ (Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire)
Trace methodology
The SRLIS (Self-Regulated Learning Interview Schedule)
mcq.e: Pintrich is tied to the MSLQ; Boekaerts to the OMQ; Zimmerman to the SRLIS; Winne to traces.

mcq.q: In Pintrich's analysis of goal orientations, what are the two main axes?
o: Individual or collective, and competitive or cooperative
Mastery or performance, and approach or avoidance
Intrinsic or extrinsic, and short-term or long-term
Cognitive or emotional, and internal or external
mcq.e: Goal orientations: mastery or performance, approach or avoidance.

mcq.q: How many stages does the Winne and Hadwin model have, and what are they?
o: Two: planning and execution
Four: forethought, monitoring, control, reflection
Four: task definition, goals and planning
Three: forethought, performance, self-reflection
mcq.e: Winne and Hadwin describe four stages with a COPES structure in each.

mcq.q: What does COPES stand for?
o: Control, Organization, Performance, Emotion, Self
Cognition, Observation, Planning, Effort, Strategy
Conditions, Operations, Products, Evaluations
Context, Outcome, Process, Evidence, Skill
mcq.e: In Winne's model each stage has a COPES structure: Conditions, Operations, Products, Evaluations, Standards.

mcq.q: What is distinctive about Winne's treatment of metacognitive monitoring?
o: Monitoring occurs only in the planning stage
Monitoring is present in every stage
Monitoring occurs only after the task is finished
Monitoring is the teacher's job, not the learner's
mcq.e: In Winne's model metacognitive monitoring appears at every stage (it is recursive).

mcq.q: Winne and colleagues (2000) compared self-reports of using seven strategies with actual traces. What did they find?
o: No correlation could be computed
A very high correlation, so self-report is enough to measure SRL
Self-reports are always lower than actual behavior
A low correlation, meaning self-reports do not accurately reflect what learners actually do
mcq.e: The paper: self-reports and traces (highlighting, writing notes) correlate low, raising a problem for relying on self-report alone.

mcq.q: What did Hadwin and colleagues (1997) find about strategy reports?
o: Students report strategies only when taking an exam
Students report the same set of strategies in all contexts
Students cannot describe their own study strategies
Students report different strategies depending on context: reading to learn, writing a short essay, exam review
mcq.e: Self-reported strategies depend on the task context, a reason for caution when generalizing.

mcq.q: What is Winne's "trace methodology"?
o: Recording learners' actual behavior while they study
An interview with teachers about students
A final exam measuring content recall
A questionnaire that learners fill in after studying
mcq.e: Traces are real behavioral records, as opposed to self-report.

mcq.q: On what theoretical base is Zimmerman's model in the review?
o: Psychoanalytic theory of the unconscious
Social cognitive theory with triadic reciprocal determinism (person, behavior, environment)
Classical behaviorism with stimulus and response
Pure information-processing theory
mcq.e: Zimmerman builds on social cognitive theory (Bandura): triadic reciprocal determinism among person, behavior and environment.

mcq.q: What are Zimmerman's four levels of SRL development?
o: Preparation, performance, reflection, adaptation
Cognition, motivation, behavior, context
Observation, emulation, self-control
Definition, planning, enactment, adaptation
mcq.e: The four levels: observation, emulation (imitation), self-control, self-regulation.

mcq.q: Which interview instrument is tied to Zimmerman and has 14 strategy categories?
o: The OMQ
The MSLQ
The SRLIS
COPES
mcq.e: The SRLIS (Self-Regulated Learning Interview Schedule) has 14 strategy categories.

mcq.q: Zimmerman and Bandura (1994) used path analysis on which skill?
o: Grade 5 mathematics
Reading comprehension
Programming
Writing
mcq.e: Zimmerman and Bandura 1994 analyzed SRL in writing achievement using path analysis.

mcq.q: According to Puustinen and Pulkkinen, which two models are the most alike?
o: Borkowski and Zimmerman
Borkowski and Winne
Boekaerts and Winne
Pintrich and Zimmerman
mcq.e: These two share a social-cognitive base, treat SRL as a goal-directed process and have similar research.

mcq.q: Which two models differ most from the rest?
o: Borkowski and Winne
Boekaerts and Pintrich
Boekaerts and Zimmerman
Pintrich and Zimmerman
mcq.e: Borkowski and Winne are far from the other models in theory; their research leans toward strategies and metacognition.

mcq.q: Which two kinds of SRL definition does the review distinguish?
o: Individual and social
Behavioral and emotional
Content-based and method-based
Goal-oriented and metacognitively weighted
mcq.e: The paper classifies definitions into goal-oriented and metacognitively weighted.

mcq.q: Which models belong to the metacognitively weighted group?
o: Pintrich and Zimmerman
Borkowski and Winne
Boekaerts and Pintrich
Boekaerts and Zimmerman
mcq.e: The metacognitively weighted definitions are tied to Borkowski and Winne.

mcq.q: What do all models in the review have in common?
o: They all apply only to primary school learners
They all ignore motivation
They run from preparation through performance to evaluation or adaptation, and all are cyclical
They all rest entirely on behaviorist theory
mcq.e: Puustinen and Pulkkinen point to a shared phase structure: preparation, performance, evaluation or adaptation, with repetition.

mcq.q: Which model is noted as concentrating on the preparatory phase and treating performance lightly?
o: Winne
Boekaerts
Zimmerman
Pintrich
mcq.e: The paper notes Boekaerts' model puts more weight on the preparatory (appraisal) phase than on performance.

mcq.q: What are the three main research orientations across the models?
o: Motivation, strategies
Individual, group, class
Memory, attention, language
Theory, experiment, application
mcq.e: Boekaerts and Pintrich lean toward motivation; Borkowski and Winne toward strategies; Zimmerman combines both.

mcq.q: Why is using a single self-report survey to measure SRL risky?
o: Because self-reports are always too expensive to collect
Because students never answer honestly
Self-reports can diverge from real behavior (Winne)
Because self-reports measure only memory ability
mcq.e: Evidence from Winne and colleagues (2000) and Hadwin and colleagues (1997) shows self-reports diverge from traces and depend on context.

mcq.q: What does combining self-report with behavioral trace data give a measurement?
o: It removes the need for any interview
It makes every learner reach the maximum score
A cross-check between what learners say
It replaces the learner's goal setting
mcq.e: Because self-reports and traces correlate weakly, using both gives a fuller picture.

mcq.q: Why is the claim "SRL is a fixed trait, you either have it or not" wrong?
o: SRL is the selective use of processes per task
Because SRL exists only in high achievers
Because SRL is determined only by external motivation
Because SRL exists only in adults
mcq.e: Zimmerman (2002) states clearly that SRL is an adaptive process, not a fixed trait.

mcq.q: Why is the claim "studying alone equals self-regulation" wrong?
o: Because studying alone is always less effective than group study
Because SRL happens only in crowded classrooms
Self-regulated learners often seek help
Because self-regulated learners never study alone
mcq.e: Zimmerman (2002) points out SRL is not asocial; seeking help is one SRL strategy.

mcq.q: Why is teaching a single strategy in isolation usually not enough?
o: Because strategies work only for young children
Learners also need to monitor outcomes
Because a single strategy cannot be learned
Because students always forget a strategy after a day
mcq.e: Zimmerman (1990) and Ghatala and colleagues show monitoring, attribution and decision-making must be taught, not only an isolated strategy.

mcq.q: In the thesis treatment model, which Zimmerman phase does "write pseudocode and predict the result before asking the AI" match?
o: Forethought: goal setting and planning
Performance: self-control through imagery
Self-reflection: self-evaluation after learning
Self-reflection: self-reaction as a defensive response
mcq.e: This is a design-inference mapping: writing a plan first is task analysis (goal setting, strategic planning) in forethought, not an empirical result.

mcq.q: Which process group does "ask the AI Socratic questions and run your own tests" match?
o: Self-judgment in the self-reflection phase
Task analysis in the forethought phase
Self-motivation beliefs in the forethought phase
Self-control and self-observation in the performance phase
mcq.e: In the design inference, interacting with the AI and self-testing are enactment (self-control) and self-tracking (self-observation).

mcq.q: Which group does "reflection and explaining back to the AI" match?
o: Task analysis in the forethought phase
Self-judgment and self-reaction in the self-reflection phase
Self-control in the performance phase
Self-experimentation in the performance phase
mcq.e: Reflecting after doing is self-judgment (evaluation, attribution) and self-reaction (adjustment) in the design inference.

mcq.q: Why record "time spent solving alone before asking the AI" when measuring SRL in the thesis?
o: Because a longer time always proves better results
It fully replaces the psychological questionnaire
It is an objective behavioral trace that complements self-report, which may diverge (Winne)
Because instructors need to grade by time
mcq.e: AI interaction logs and solo solving time are traces that complement self-report in the spirit of Winne (a design inference for the thesis).

mcq.q: How does the thesis idea of "fading" relate to Zimmerman's four development levels?
o: Fading means gradually increasing the amount of AI hints over time
Fading applies only to the initial observation level
From observation and emulation (the AI as a model) to self-control
Fading does not relate to any level
mcq.e: A design inference linking Modules 03 and 04: withdrawing support corresponds to moving from the observation and emulation levels to the self-control and self-regulation levels.

mcq.q: If the treatment group improves scores but does not reflect on strategy, what does Zimmerman's model predict?
o: The cycle is still complete because performance was good
Self-efficacy rises automatically without reflection
Learners move into a different forethought phase
The cycle is left open: without reflection the next preparation does not improve durably
mcq.e: In the cyclical model self-reflection feeds forethought; without it, learning does not accumulate from one attempt to the next (inferred from the model).

mcq.q: In the thesis mapping, in which phase does "self-efficacy" appear in Zimmerman's model?
o: Performance, as a self-control strategy
It does not appear in any model
Forethought, as a self-motivation belief
Self-reflection, as a defensive reaction
mcq.e: Self-efficacy belongs to the self-motivation beliefs of forethought; it is also fed back by self-reflection (Module 06 goes deeper).

mcq.q: Which of the following should be avoided when concluding about AI's effect on SRL?
o: Using a control group and repeated measures
Drawing causal conclusions from a one-time self-report survey with no control group
Reporting both effect sizes and confidence intervals
Combining self-report with behavioral data
mcq.e: Zimmerman and Puustinen and Pulkkinen both stress the limits of self-report; causal claims need experimental design (Module 13).

mcq.q: Which limitation of Puustinen and Pulkkinen (2001) should be noted when using it as a base for the thesis?
o: The paper deals only with preschool children
The paper has never been peer reviewed
It is a 2001 review, before the wave of generative AI, so it must be supplemented with newer research
The paper describes no specific model
mcq.e: The review reflects 1990s understanding and does not discuss generative AI; this is my note on the timing limitation.

essay.q: Present the three phases of Zimmerman's model and give a programming-learning example for each process group (task analysis, motivation beliefs, self-control, self-observation, self-judgment, self-reaction).
essay.m: Hint: Forethought: set the goal "pass three test cases", plan a strategy (write pseudocode); self-efficacy, interest. Performance: self-control (split into small functions, focus), self-observation (record the number of failed runs, experiment with edge cases). Self-reflection: self-evaluation against the goal and against the previous level, attribution (strategy versus ability), adaptive reaction (change the debugging approach) versus defensive (give up the task). The examples are design inference.

essay.q: Compare novices and experts according to Zimmerman (2002) on goals, self-evaluation standards, attribution and emotional consequences, and state what happens when AI removes the chance to practice these processes.
essay.m: Hint: Novice: vague goals, compare with others, attribute to lack of ability, less satisfied. Expert: hierarchical goals, compare with own goals, attribute to strategy, more satisfied. If the AI does the planning and self-evaluating for students, they do not practice these processes; this is a hypothesis that must be measured (Module 13).

essay.q: Analyze the evidence for the three features of SRL in Zimmerman (1990): state the figures 93%, r = .70 and nearly 80% of variance, and their limits.
essay.m: Hint: 93% correct track classification on 80 students (50% by chance); an SRL factor with nearly 80% of the variance of teacher-rated scores; r = .70 with self-report (r² = .49). Limits: small sample, one school, correlational data do not prove causation, self-reports diverge from behavior (Winne), 1980s age and context.

essay.q: Compare the Zimmerman and Winne models on theoretical base, unit of analysis and measurement, then choose the one better suited to a thesis on teaching programming with AI and explain why.
essay.m: Hint: Zimmerman: social cognitive, three phases, SRLIS interview, emphasis on motivation and self-efficacy. Winne: information processing, four COPES stages, monitoring at every phase, behavioral traces. For the thesis: Zimmerman gives the psychological frame (RQ2: self-efficacy, confidence), Winne the behavior measurement (RQ3: logs, traces). They can be combined; the choice is a design inference.

essay.q: Design how you would measure SRL in your thesis, naming at least one self-report instrument, one behavioral (trace) indicator, and how you would check whether the two kinds of data agree.
essay.m: Hint: Self-report: the MSLQ (Pintrich) or an SRLIS-style interview. Behavioral indicators: time solving alone before asking the AI, number of self-run tests, types of questions sent to the AI, number of code edits after a hint. Compare by correlating self-report scores with behavioral indicators; a low correlation as in Winne 2000 is a sign to report transparently, not hide.

essay.q: What are four common misconceptions about SRL (fixed trait, asocial, self-report only, one strategy is enough)? Explain why each is wrong and what it implies for designing a programming class.
essay.m: Hint: Fixed is wrong because SRL is a teachable process; asocial is wrong because seeking help is an SRL strategy (asking peers, asking the AI on purpose); self-report only is wrong because it diverges from behavior; one strategy is enough is wrong because monitoring and decisions are needed. Implications: teach the three phases systematically, build in reflection, keep logs, and balance the three dimensions (metacognition, motivation, behavior).
